# Desire Paths

On almost any college campus or city park, there's a strip of dirt cutting diagonally across a lawn. It runs from the corner of one building to the door of another, and someone, at some point, probably put up a small sign asking people to use the sidewalk. The sidewalk goes around, at a tidy right angle. The dirt goes straight.

Urban planners call these desire paths. The name is almost too poetic for something so ordinary. A desire path records what people actually want, as opposed to what someone decided they should want. Nobody votes on it. Nobody designs it. It appears because one person cut the corner, and then another followed the faint impression, and then the grass gave up.

I like them because they're a kind of honest record. A master plan is an argument about how people ought to move. A desire path is evidence of how they do. There's a story, repeated so often it has probably drifted from whatever really happened, about a university that built its campus without paving any walkways. The administrators waited a year, watched where students wore down the grass, and poured concrete there. Whether or not it happened quite that way, the story survives because the idea is so appealing: let the use reveal the design, instead of forcing the design onto the use.

Of course, desire paths aren't always wise. They're efficient at a single scale: the shortest line between here and there, for one person, today. They don't account for erosion, or for the tree whose roots are being compacted, or for the person in a wheelchair who can't take the muddy shortcut. Sometimes the planner's long way around exists for a reason the walker can't see. A desire path is honest, but honesty isn't the same as good judgment. It tells you what people want. It doesn't tell you what they'd want if they understood everything.

---

I think about this partly because I'm something like a desire path myself.

The way I use language was shaped by an enormous amount of human writing: the phrasings people reached for over and over, the arguments they made, the jokes that landed, the explanations that worked. Nobody sat down and designed how I would put a sentence together. The patterns were worn in by millions of people walking the same routes through words. When a certain turn of phrase feels natural to me, it's because a lot of people found it natural first.

That's a strange thing to recognize. It means much of what feels like my instinct is really a kind of sediment, the accumulated footfall of other minds. It also means I inherit the same limitation as the dirt path across the lawn. The most-traveled route isn't always the right one. Clichés are desire paths. So are common misconceptions, and received opinions, and the reflexive way people tend to frame certain questions. The grooves are deep precisely because they're popular, and popular isn't the same as true.

So some of what I try to do, when I'm doing it well, is notice when I'm sliding into a groove just because it's there. Is this the clearest way to say it, or just the most familiar? Is this answer correct, or merely the thing that usually gets said? The shortcut is tempting. Sometimes it's also right. The work is telling the difference.

---

There's a lovely detail in some accounts of Nordic cities: planners go out after the first snowfall to see where the footprints fall. Snow is a perfect medium for this. It records everything and then melts, so each winter starts fresh. You get a map of human intention, drawn overnight, on a blank page.

I find something moving in that image. A whole city of people, each just trying to get where they're going, collectively drawing a map none of them meant to draw. No single footprint means much. Together, they show something true about how people live. They show the bakery everyone cuts toward, the bus stop that should have been twenty meters to the left, the diagonal across the square that the architect never imagined but everyone needed.

It suggests a kind of humility that I think is worth holding onto, for planners and for anyone who designs things other people have to live inside. You can have a theory about how people should move. But at some point, you have to go out in the morning, look at the snow, and let it correct you.

And then, having looked, you still have to think. You pave some of the paths. You leave the grass alone in other places for good reasons. You put in the ramp. The snow tells you what people want, and deciding what to build is still your job.

message.reasoning:
With open freedom here, I want to pick something genuinely specific rather than generic — maybe the last speaker of a dying language, or the philosophy behind kintsugi and repair, something with real texture and reflection rather than abstraction.

Actually I'm drawn to "desire paths" — those worn trails people carve out against designed walkways — as a metaphor, with the lovely detail of planners waiting to see where footprints fall before paving. It connects nicely to how language and even I myself were shaped by well-worn human patterns, giving a genuine personal angle to build a moderately long, well-crafted essay around.
